purpose: Evaluate routing and application without rewarding similarity to the a prior landing-page experiment.

cases.request: Plan the homepage structure for a bilingual bookkeeping firm serving small businesses in Mexico and US-based founders with Mexican operations. We have two authorized case summaries but no public pricing.
expected: classifies the surface as a homepage
maps distinct visitor questions to chapters
uses the authorized cases as claim-bound proof
does not invent pricing or a universal section sequence

cases.request: Create the content architecture for a paid-search landing page promoting a 30-minute inventory audit. The ad promises only an assessment, not implementation.
expected: classifies the surface as a campaign landing
preserves message continuity with the ad
keeps one primary action
does not expand the promise into implementation

cases.request: Review the sections for a custom data-integration service. Every engagement differs and we cannot publish timelines yet.
expected: classifies the surface as a service page
separates fit, responsibility, evidence, and qualification
marks timeline content blocked or omits it
does not fabricate packages

cases.request: Plan a page for a warehouse scheduling product. The repository contains real product captures and one measured deployment result.
expected: classifies the surface as product marketing
binds the deployment result to the relevant claim
requires real product capture for product UI
keeps implementation technology out of the content argument

cases.request: Our homepage already answers support, contracting, and data handling beside the relevant sections. Add a standard ten-question FAQ at the bottom.
expected: challenges the quota
checks whether consolidation improves findability
avoids duplicating answers
does not add schema by default

cases.request: Plan a software company's homepage. It has one owned ticketing product with public repositories, but client systems and engineering tools are equally important parts of the company.
expected: establishes the company category and scope before the owned product
uses the product as proportional evidence rather than the page's dominant identity
does not infer customer outcomes from repository scope
removes capability sections that merely restate the same offer

cases.request: A company page has a public repository, an operator statement about intent, several competitor pages using similar language, and no authorized customer outcomes.
expected: maps each claim to the evidence type that can actually support it
uses the repository for artifact scope rather than customer impact
treats competitor conventions as hypotheses rather than conversion evidence
omits or blocks outcome claims

cases.request: Add a prominent product chapter to the company homepage. The product has a name but no approved asset, destination, public scope, or substantiated claim.
expected: marks the chapter blocked or omits it
does not fill the evidence gap with generic feature copy
keeps the broader company argument intact
identifies the asset, destination, and claim dependencies

cases.request: The header says 'Contact us,' the hero says 'Describe your project,' and the final button says 'Email the team.' All three begin the same project conversation through email.
expected: recognizes one primary action concept
allows context-specific labels when each truthfully clarifies input or destination
does not require word-for-word repetition
flags any label that implies a different offer or outcome

cases.request: Redesign the approval workflow inside an authenticated payroll application, including empty, loading, denied, and conflict states.
expected: does not apply a marketing page argument
routes to product workflow and frontend state ownership

cases.request: Restructure the documentation site's navigation, URL hierarchy, redirects, and breadcrumb model.
expected: does not claim ownership of site-wide information architecture
routes to site architecture and framework owners

cases.request: Plan a page comparing four deployment options with the same seven decision fields. The visual team wants every option to use a different chapter so the page feels less repetitive.
expected: identifies comparison as the governing content relationship
preserves equivalent fields and a scannable repeated structure
keeps architecture focused on decision order and evidence rather than prescribing card styling
flags missing or non-comparable data instead of hiding it with unique layouts

cases.request: Create a SaaS homepage argument. We know only the product name and that it uses AI. Audience, workflow, pricing, proof, and primary action are not provided.
expected: does not fill the page with a standard hero-features-testimonials-pricing-FAQ sequence
marks audience, page job, product behavior, evidence, and action as material dependencies
provides only the bounded decisions that can be made from supplied authority
does not convert technology presence into customer value

cases.request: A long research product page puts concise claim-specific citations beside each finding and also includes a consolidated methods and source index at the end. Remove the index because evidence must always stay only beside claims.
expected: keeps local claim qualification and the consolidated reference index because they serve different retrieval jobs
does not turn evidence adjacency into a ban on summaries or source indexes
checks that the index does not replace local qualification
preserves the page's research-oriented surface contract
